triples.source_text: The Lord showed me this: Look, a brood of locusts was coming at dawn, and look, one bruchus locust, Gog the king.

target_units.text: What the caterpillar left, the locust devoured; what the locust left, the bruchus locust devoured; what the bruchus locust left, the blight devoured.

triples.relationship: locust and bruchus imagery in agricultural devastation
triples.rationale: Amos's vision presents a brood of locusts and a bruchus locust, followed in the next verse by devouring the land's grass. Joel likewise names locust and bruchus among successive devourers of what remains. This connection concerns the insects and their devastation, without identifying Amos's Gog label with another figure.

triples.source_text: When it finishes devouring the land’s grass, I said, “Lord, Lord, be merciful! Who will raise Jacob? He is so few!

target_units.text: In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”
Then the Lord became jealous for His land and spared His people.

triples.relationship: intercession for the people amid threatened devastation
triples.rationale: Amos pleads for mercy for Jacob, who is so few, as the locust vision reaches the land's grass. Joel's priests likewise ask the Lord to spare His people, followed by His sparing them. Both put an appeal for the people's preservation before the Lord.

triples.source_text: Relent, Lord, concerning this.” “This will not happen,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: Let not the Egyptians say, ‘He led them out with evil intent, to kill them in the mountains and consume them from the earth.’ Cease from Thy fierce anger and be merciful concerning Thy people’s evil,

remembering Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Thy servants, to whom Thou didst swear by Thyself and speak, saying, ‘I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of heaven in multitude’; and all this land which Thou didst say Thou wouldest give to their seed, they shall possess for ever.”
The Lord was appeased concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon His people.

triples.relationship: appeal for mercy followed by withdrawal of announced calamity
triples.rationale: Amos's plea that the Lord relent is answered with the declaration that this will not happen. Moses likewise asks the Lord to cease from fierce anger and be merciful, after which the Lord is appeased concerning the calamity announced against His people.

triples.source_text: The Lord showed me this: Look, the Lord called for judgment by fire; it devoured the great abyss and devoured the portion.

target_units.text: For a fire has been kindled out of My wrath; it shall burn unto Hades beneath, devour the earth and its produce, and set ablaze the foundations of the mountains.

triples.relationship: divine judgment by fire reaching the depths
triples.rationale: Amos sees judgment by fire devouring the great abyss and the portion. Deuteronomy likewise describes fire kindled from divine wrath, burning to Hades beneath and devouring the earth and its produce. The connection is the fire's destructive reach, without equating the abyss with Hades.

triples.source_text: I said, “Lord, Lord, cease, please! Who will raise Jacob? He is so few!

target_units.text: When it finishes devouring the land’s grass, I said, “Lord, Lord, be merciful! Who will raise Jacob? He is so few!

triples.relationship: same-chapter repeated plea for Jacob's preservation
triples.rationale: Both appeals address the Lord and ask who will raise Jacob because he is so few. The first asks for mercy after the locust vision; the second asks Him to cease after the fire vision, repeating the reason for intercession.

triples.source_text: Relent, Lord, concerning this.” “This certainly will not happen,” says the Lord.

target_units.text: Relent, Lord, concerning this.” “This will not happen,” says the Lord.

triples.relationship: same-chapter repeated answer to intercession
triples.rationale: Both units follow a plea to relent with the Lord's declaration that the threatened event will not happen. The repeated answer links the locust and fire visions while preserving the second answer's emphatic wording.

triples.source_text: The Lord said to me, “What do you see, Amos?” I said, “Adamant.” The Lord said to me, “Look, I am setting adamant in the midst of My people Israel. I will certainly no longer pass them by,

target_units.text: He said, “What do you see, Amos?” I said, “A fowler’s vessel.” The Lord said to me, “The end has arrived upon My people Israel. I will certainly no longer pass them by.

triples.relationship: same-book vision question and repeated judgment refrain
triples.rationale: Both visions ask Amos what he sees, receive his answer naming the object, and end with the Lord declaring that He will no longer pass His people by. The objects remain distinct: adamant in chapter 7 and a fowler's vessel in chapter 8.

triples.source_text: and the altars of laughter will disappear, and Israel’s rites will be laid waste. I will rise against Jeroboam’s house with a sword.”

target_units.text: The shrines of On, Israel’s sins, will be removed; thorns and thistles will grow on their altars. They will say to the mountains, ‘Cover us!’ and to the hills, ‘Fall upon us!’

triples.relationship: judgment on Israel's altars and rites
triples.rationale: Amos announces that the altars of laughter will disappear and Israel's rites be laid waste. Hosea likewise announces removal of the shrines of On, described as Israel's sins, and thorns and thistles upon their altars. Both announce the ruin of places of worship without equating their different labels.

triples.source_text: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, “Amos is forming conspiracies against you in the midst of Israel’s house. The land certainly cannot endure all his words,

target_units.text: And when Jeremiah stopped speaking everything the Lord commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests, false prophets, and all the people seized him, saying: You must die!
Because you prophesied in the Lord’s name, saying, This house will be like Shiloh and this city will be emptied of inhabitants. And all the people assembled against Jeremiah in the Lord’s house.
And Judah’s rulers heard this word and went up from the king’s house to the Lord’s house. They sat before the Lord’s New Gate.
And the priests and false prophets said to the rulers and all the people: A sentence of death for this man, because he prophesied against this city, as you heard with your own ears!

triples.relationship: religious officials accuse a prophet before political authorities
triples.rationale: Amaziah the priest reports Amos to Israel's king, alleging conspiracy and intolerable words. In Jeremiah, priests and false prophets likewise complain to the rulers about his prophecy against the city and demand death. Both accounts show opposition to a prophet's message being brought before governing authorities.

triples.source_text: because Amos says, ‘Jeroboam will die by a sword, and Israel will be led captive away from its land.’”

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘Your wife will practice prostitution in the city, your sons and daughters will fall by a sword, and your land will be measured out with a cord. You will die in an unclean land, and Israel will be led captive away from its land.’”

triples.relationship: same-chapter recurrence of Israel's captivity prediction
triples.rationale: Amaziah's report attributes to Amos the prediction that Israel will be led captive away from its land. The later word addressed to Amaziah ends with that same prediction. This link concerns the captivity clause, without treating Amaziah's separate claim about Jeroboam's individual death as independently verified.

triples.source_text: Amaziah said to Amos, “Seer, go! Withdraw to Judah’s land; make your living there, and there you will prophesy.

target_units.text: At that very hour some Pharisees approached and said to Him, “Leave and go away from here, because Herod wants to kill Thee.”
And He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I drive out demons and accomplish healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion.’
Nevertheless, I must travel today and tomorrow and the day following, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.

triples.relationship: pressure on a prophetic speaker to leave
triples.rationale: Amaziah tells Amos to withdraw to Judah, where he may make his living and prophesy. In Luke, Jesus is urged to leave because Herod wants to kill Him, and He answers in terms of a prophet's journey toward Jerusalem. Both passages place a demand to leave beside the prophetic mission, with different stated reasons.

triples.source_text: But you must never again prophesy at Bethel, because it is a king’s sanctuary and a house of kingship.”

target_units.text: They called them in and ordered them neither to speak nor to teach at all in the name of Jesus.
Peter and John answered them, “Judge whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God;
for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”

triples.relationship: prohibition of public proclamation met by duty to God
triples.rationale: Amaziah prohibits Amos from prophesying at the royal sanctuary of Bethel. The council similarly prohibits Peter and John from speaking or teaching in Jesus' name, while they answer that they must speak what they have seen and heard. Amos's following reply likewise grounds his mission in the Lord's command.

triples.source_text: Amos answered Amaziah, “I was no prophet or prophet’s son, but a goat herder and one who scratches sycamore figs,

target_units.text: On that day the prophets will be ashamed, each because of his vision when he prophesies; they will wear a hairy skin because they lied.
He will say, ‘I am no prophet; I am a man who works the earth, because a man begot me from my youth.’

triples.relationship: contrasting uses of a denial of prophetic status and an agricultural occupation
triples.rationale: Amos says he was no prophet or prophet's son but a goat herder and sycamore-fig worker, before recounting the Lord's call. Zechariah's speaker likewise denies being a prophet and names work on the earth, in a context of prophets ashamed of lying. The verbal pattern is shared while the contexts and purposes differ.

triples.source_text: and the Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’

target_units.text: Now say this to My servant David: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I took you from the sheepfold to be ruler over My people, over Israel,

triples.relationship: the Lord takes a person from tending sheep to service over Israel
triples.rationale: Amos says the Lord took him from the sheep and commanded him to prophesy to His people Israel. The word to David likewise recalls the Lord taking him from the sheepfold to be ruler over Israel. The call from the flock is shared, while prophecy and kingship remain distinct tasks.

triples.source_text: Now hear the Lord’s word: You say, ‘Do not prophesy against Israel, and you must not stir up a crowd against Jacob’s house.’

target_units.text: For this is a disobedient people, lying sons who did not want to hear God’s law,
who say to the prophets, “Do not announce to us,” and to those seeing visions, “Do not speak to us. Instead, speak to us and announce another deception,
and turn us from this way, remove this path from us, and remove Israel’s Holy One from us.”

triples.relationship: opposition to unwelcome prophetic speech
triples.rationale: Amos repeats the prohibition on prophesying against Israel and stirring up a crowd against Jacob's house. Isaiah likewise describes a disobedient people telling prophets and visionaries not to announce or speak, asking instead for deception. Both passages report attempts to suppress unwelcome prophetic speech.

triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: ‘Your wife will practice prostitution in the city, your sons and daughters will fall by a sword, and your land will be measured out with a cord. You will die in an unclean land, and Israel will be led captive away from its land.’”

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord: Behold, I am giving you to migration with all your friends. They will fall by their enemies’ sword, and your eyes will see. I will give you and all Judah into the hands of Babylon’s king, and they will deport them and cut them down with swords.
And I will give all this city’s strength, all its labors, and all the treasures of Judah’s king into his enemies’ hands, and they will bring them to Babylon.
And you and all who dwell in your house will go into captivity. In Babylon you will die and there be buried—you and all your friends to whom you prophesied false things.

triples.relationship: a priest opposing a prophet is warned of sword, captivity and death abroad
triples.rationale: Amos's response to Amaziah announces deaths by sword, captivity and his death in an unclean land. Jeremiah's response to Pashhur likewise announces sword deaths among his associates and captivity ending in his death in Babylon. The surrounding accounts identify each opponent as a priest who acts against the prophet.

triples.source_text: He said, “What do you see, Amos?” I said, “A fowler’s vessel.” The Lord said to me, “The end has arrived upon My people Israel. I will certainly no longer pass them by.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, say, ‘Thus says the Lord to the land of Israel: An end has come; the end has come upon the four wings of the land.
The end has come
upon you, inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day has drawn near, neither with tumult nor with birth pangs.

triples.relationship: the announced arrival of an end upon Israel
triples.rationale: Amos's vision is explained by the declaration that the end has arrived upon the Lord's people Israel. Ezekiel likewise addresses Israel's land with the repeated declaration that an end has come upon it and its inhabitants. Both declare the arrival of an end in a judgment oracle.

triples.source_text: Hear these things now, you who wear out the needy until morning and oppress the poor out of the land,

target_units.text: Do not use force against the needy, for he is poor, and do not dishonor the weak at the gates;
for the Lord will judge his case, and you will preserve your own life unplundered.

triples.relationship: oppression of the needy opposed to the prohibition of force
triples.rationale: Amos addresses those who wear out the needy and oppress the poor out of the land. Proverbs explicitly forbids force against the needy and dishonoring the weak, adding that the Lord will judge the poor person's case.

triples.source_text: saying, “When will the month pass, so we may trade, and the sabbaths, so we may open storehouses, making the measure small and the weights great and making an unjust balance,

target_units.text: You shall not have in your pouch differing weights, a great and a small.
You shall not have in your house differing measures, a great and a small.
You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you for a possession.
For everyone who does these things, everyone who does injustice, is an abomination unto the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: unjust commercial measurements opposed to the legal standard
triples.rationale: Amos reports traders planning a small measure, great weights and an unjust balance. Deuteronomy forbids differing weights and measures, requires true and just ones, and condemns those who practice that injustice.

triples.source_text: to acquire the poor with silver and a lowly person in exchange for sandals? And we will trade from every kind of produce.”

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals,

triples.relationship: same-book exchange of vulnerable people for silver and sandals
triples.rationale: Amos 8 reports an intention to acquire poor people for silver and a lowly person for sandals. Amos 2 condemns selling a righteous person for silver and a poor person for sandals. The repeated prices connect buying and selling within the book's accusations of exploitation.

triples.source_text: The Lord swears by Jacob’s arrogance: “He will never forget all your works.”

target_units.text: so that they sing together as people singing together with their heart. I remembered all their evils; now their schemes have surrounded them; they have come before My face.

triples.relationship: wrongdoing remembered before God
triples.rationale: Following the charges of oppression and unjust trade, the oath in Amos declares that the people's works will never be forgotten. Hosea likewise speaks of all their evils remembered and their schemes coming before the Lord's face. Amos's oath by Jacob's arrogance is preserved without changing its stated object.

triples.source_text: Will the earth not be disturbed over these things, and everyone dwelling in it mourn? A consummation will rise like a river and descend like Egypt’s river.

target_units.text: The Lord, Lord God Almighty, touches the earth and shakes it; all who dwell in it will mourn. Its consummation will rise like a river and descend like Egypt’s river.

triples.relationship: same-book recurrence of earth's disturbance and Egypt's river
triples.rationale: Both passages join the disturbed or shaken earth with its inhabitants mourning and a consummation rising like a river and descending like Egypt's river. Amos 9 explicitly introduces the Lord touching the earth within this repeated description.

triples.source_text: “On that day,” says the Lord God, “the sun will set at midday, and the light will grow dark upon the earth in daytime.

target_units.text: She who bore seven was emptied; her soul grew faint. Her sun set while the day was still at its middle; she was ashamed and reproached. Their remnants I will give to the sword before their enemies.

triples.relationship: sunset during the middle of the day as judgment imagery
triples.rationale: Amos announces the sun setting at midday and daylight growing dark upon the earth. Jeremiah likewise describes the sun of the woman who bore seven setting while the day is still at its middle, beside shame and threatened sword deaths. Both use the unexpected midday sunset in a judgment setting.

triples.source_text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

target_units.text: Daughter of My people, gird yourself with sackcloth; sprinkle yourself with ashes. Make mourning for yourself for a beloved one, a pitiful lament, because misery will suddenly come upon you.

triples.relationship: sackcloth and mourning for a beloved one
triples.rationale: Amos joins sackcloth with lamentation and mourning for a beloved one. Jeremiah likewise tells the daughter of the people to wear sackcloth and make a pitiful lament for a beloved one because misery is coming.

triples.source_text: I will turn your festivals to mourning and all your songs to lamentation. I will put sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head; I will make him like mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of pain.

target_units.text: and they will gird on sackcloth; amazement will cover them, shame will be upon every face among them, and baldness upon every head.

triples.relationship: shared public mourning signs of sackcloth and baldness
triples.rationale: Amos announces sackcloth on every waist and baldness on every head. Ezekiel likewise describes people girding on sackcloth, shame upon every face and baldness upon every head. Both extend these mourning signs across the judged population.

triples.source_text: Look, days are coming,” says the Lord, “when I will send famine upon the earth: not famine for bread or thirst for water, but famine for hearing the Lord’s word.

target_units.text: And He afflicted you, and made you hunger, and fed you with manna, which your fathers did not know, that He might declare unto you that man shall not live by bread alone, but man shall live by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God.

triples.relationship: bread and the Lord's word distinguished as human necessities
triples.rationale: Amos announces a famine for hearing the Lord's word rather than for bread or water. Deuteronomy recounts hunger and manna to explain that a person lives by every word from God's mouth and not by bread alone. Both distinguish dependence on God's word from physical bread.

triples.source_text: Waters will be shaken as far as the sea, and from north to east they will run about seeking the Lord’s word, but certainly will not find it.

target_units.text: Saul saw the foreigners’ camp and was afraid, and his heart was greatly astounded.
Saul inquired through the Lord, but the Lord did not answer him by dreams, by clear signs, or by prophets.

triples.relationship: seeking divine communication without receiving an answer
triples.rationale: Amos describes people running about seeking the Lord's word but not finding it. Samuel's account describes Saul inquiring through the Lord while receiving no answer through dreams, clear signs or prophets. Both describe an unsuccessful search for divine communication, in different settings.

triples.source_text: On that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will faint from thirst,

target_units.text: The nursing child’s tongue clung to its throat with thirst. Infants asked for bread; there is no one to break it for them.

triples.relationship: young people pictured with thirst in calamity
triples.rationale: Amos foretells young women and men fainting from thirst. Lamentations portrays a nursing child's tongue clinging to its throat with thirst, alongside infants asking for bread. Both use images of bodily thirst among the young, while the age groups and exact effects differ.

triples.source_text: those who swear by Samaria’s propitiation and say, ‘Your god lives, Dan!’ and ‘Your god lives, Beersheba!’ They will fall and certainly never rise again.”

target_units.text: The king took counsel, went, and made two golden heifers. He said to the people, “Let your going up to Jerusalem be enough. Behold, your gods, Israel, who brought you up from Egypt!”
He placed one in Bethel and put the other in Dan.
This matter became a sin. The people went before the one as far as Dan.

triples.relationship: the condemned cult of Dan and its golden heifer
triples.rationale: Amos condemns people who declare that Dan's god lives. Kings records one of the two golden heifers being placed in Dan and calls the resulting practice a sin. The connection concerns Dan's cult; Amos's separate wording about Samaria's propitiation and Beersheba remains unchanged.

and say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Gog, ruler of Rhos, Mosoch and Thobel,
and I will gather you and all your force, horses and horsemen all clothed in breastplates, a great assembly, small shields, helmets and swords,

target_units.text: Behold, I have made your face strong against their faces, and I will strengthen your contention against their contention,
and it will always be stronger than rock. Do not fear them or be terrified before their faces, for it is an embittering house.”

unresolved_candidates.reason: Amos explicitly describes adamant in a wall and a hand. The supplied Ezekiel text instead speaks of a strengthened face and contention stronger than rock. It does not name adamant or a wall; the proposed particular material correspondence is not retained.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: The Lord showed me this: Look, a fowler’s vessel.

target_units.text: Like a set trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit; therefore they became great and rich.

An identification of the two images and their functions was not established beyond the general fowling association, so the proposal is unretained.
